title: The gospels written down
hook: as eyewitnesses aged, their memories were written as the four gospels

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hosea's mercy not sacrifice, and your line was pray for the peace of jerusalem. Did you stop for a breath before scrolling on? Today, what the church did with its memories. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

Who in your family still remembers the oldest stories? The grandmother who knows how your great-grandparents met. The uncle who was there when the house burned. A lot of families have someone like that, and sooner or later somebody says: we should write this down. The early church had that moment too. The people who had walked with Jesus wouldn't be there forever. A letter in Peter's name says it plainly: "I will endeavour that ye may be able after my decease to have these things always in remembrance." The stories were still told aloud, at tables and in prayers, but the voices were thinning. Today is about the decision to put the memories on paper, and what one writer says about why.

Luke opens his Gospel like a careful historian, and in the King James Bible it reads: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us, Even as they delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word." Notice what he admits. He isn't the first to try. Others have written already. And the stories came from eyewitnesses who delivered them, handed them on, the way tradition works. Luke says he's going to write it "in order," so that his friend Theophilus might "know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed." Mark starts with no introduction at all: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." Straight in. An early tradition, preserved by the church historian Eusebius, says Mark wrote down what Peter remembered. John ends with a confession: there's far more than this. "And many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book: But these are written, that ye might believe." And at the very end, almost with a smile: if everything were written down, "even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written." So the church ended up with four Gospels, under the names tradition gives them: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. They tell the same Jesus from four angles, and they don't always line up in detail. In the end the churches kept all four side by side instead of blending them into one. Four accounts, each in its own voice, written down before they forget.
screen: `THESE ARE WRITTEN, THAT YE MIGHT BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write down one story from an elder. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone older who told you a story more than once: a parent, a grandparent, a neighbor, a teacher. Let one story come back. Where were they? Who was there? What did they say at the end? Then, if you have something to write with, put it down in a few lines, plain, the way they told it. Don't polish it. If you pray, you can give thanks for the person who told it. The bell holds the time.
Luke. The evangelist who wrote his gospel in order, so Theophilus might know the certainty of what he'd been taught, as the church set its eyewitness memories on paper.
Your line: before they forget. Today, ask one older person to tell you a story you've never heard, and write it down. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Churches read from the Gospels in their services, often standing for the reading, and in several churches the reading plan moves through Matthew, Mark and Luke over a cycle of years, with John read at special seasons.

fork.setup: you're an early church leader. the eyewitnesses are dying. people tell the stories at every meal, a little differently. what do you do?
options: let the stories stay spoken; writing will spoil them.
write them down, from those who were there.
choose one version and forbid the rest.
fork.reveal: Luke writes "in order," from what eyewitnesses delivered, and the church keeps four Gospels side by side.

original.note: Greek: gospel, good news; the word in Mark 1:1.

trapdoor: what you thought: the gospels were written as the story happened.
what it means: eyewitnesses told the stories, and as they aged, the memories were written down.
what a scholar hears: Luke 1:1–4 names earlier written accounts and eyewitnesses who delivered the story, the same idea of handing on as tradition.
recall: let the exiles go home to build

notes: Editor pass: 'kept all four instead of blending them' softened with 'in the end' to allow for harmonies such as the Diatessaron.
John 20:30 in the KJV begins 'And many other signs'; the script quotes from 'many other signs' with a capital M. Confirm the trimmed quotation is acceptable.
No dates or authorship claims are made beyond 'the names tradition gives them' and the Papias tradition (via Eusebius 3.39) that Mark wrote down Peter's memories. Confirm.
'They don't always line up in detail' is a statement about the texts; churches explain the differences in different ways. Confirm tone.
'Kept all four side by side instead of blending them into one': harmonies such as Tatian's Diatessaron existed and were used in some churches for a time; consider softening.
howItsDone mentions a reading plan moving through Matthew, Mark and Luke over a cycle of years (the three-year Revised Common and Catholic lectionaries). Confirm.
Original: εὐαγγέλιον; the gloss 'good news' is the standard lexical sense. Confirm.

Second editor pass: unsourced 'growing old; some had died' replaced with Acts 12:2 (James killed with the sword, added to sources as a paraphrase); John 20:30 quotation now begins exactly as the KJV ('And many other signs').

Audit pass: 'four witnesses, each remembering' contradicted Luke 1:2 (Luke writes from what eyewitnesses delivered); now 'four accounts'. The hook's Acts 12:2 (James killed with the sword) repeated day 747; replaced with 2 Peter 1:15 (KJV), attributed to 'a letter in Peter's name' since authorship is debated.
